n: The Book of Moses comes from Joseph Smith’s inspired revision of the Bible (JST). This first chapter, revealed in June 1830, has no counterpart in Genesis. It records an experience Moses had on a very high mountain, after the burning bush but before he led Israel out of Egypt.

f.w: caught up into an exceedingly high mountain

f.g: Revealed to Joseph Smith in June 1830 as he began his inspired revision of the Bible.

n: Moses saw God face to face and talked with him. He could survive God’s presence only because God’s glory rested on him and changed him.

f.w: he saw God face to face
the glory of God was upon Moses

n: God introduces himself as the Almighty, whose name is “Endless”—without beginning or end.
The first truth God teaches Moses: “Thou art my son.” Before showing him creation, God establishes Moses’ divine identity. His works and words never cease.
No one can see all God’s works without seeing all his glory—and no mortal could see all his glory and remain mortal.
God has a work for Moses. Moses is made in the likeness of the Only Begotten—Jesus Christ—who is and will be the Savior, full of grace and truth. All things are present before God.

f.w: in the similitude of mine Only Begotten
f.g: Similitude = likeness; Moses’ life would foreshadow Christ’s as deliverer and lawgiver.

f.w: all things are present with me

n: God shows Moses “one thing”—a view of this world—because Moses is in the world.

f.w: this one thing I show unto thee
f.g: A limited view, suited to Moses’ mortal role.

n: Moses sees the earth from end to end and all its people, past and present, and is filled with wonder.
When God’s presence withdrew, Moses was left alone in his natural state and collapsed to the ground.

After hours of recovery, Moses realizes that “man is nothing” compared to God—something he had never imagined. Yet God has just called him a son. Both truths—our smallness and our divine worth—belong together.
Moses explains he saw God with spiritual, not natural, eyes—he was transfigured, or temporarily changed, so he could endure God’s presence.

f.g: Transfigured = temporarily changed by God’s power to withstand his glory.

n: Immediately Satan comes, calling Moses “son of man” and demanding worship. Notice Satan’s first move: attacking Moses’ identity as a son of God.

f.w: Moses, son of man, worship me

n: Moses answers boldly: I am a son of God, like his Only Begotten. Where is your glory that I should worship you? Knowing who he is protects him.

f.w: I am a son of God

f.g: Satan has no true glory to compare with God’s.

n: Moses points out the contrast: he needed to be transfigured to see God, but he can look at Satan with ordinary eyes.
Satan’s “glory” is darkness to Moses. He can tell the difference between God and Satan, remembering God’s command to worship God alone.

f.w: I can judge between thee and God
Worship God, for him only shalt thou serve

n: “Get thee hence, Satan; deceive me not”—Moses rebukes him, again relying on God’s words about his identity.
Moses recalls the burning bush, where God taught him to call upon God in the name of the Only Begotten.

f.w: in the name of mine Only Begotten

n: Moses refuses to stop praying; he has more to ask. Having felt God’s glory, he can tell God and Satan apart.

f.w: I will not cease to call upon God

n: Satan throws a tantrum, raging and shouting, “I am the Only Begotten, worship me!”—a blatant lie claiming Christ’s place.

f.g: Spoke or shouted wildly and angrily.

f.w: I am the Only Begotten, worship me

n: Moses becomes frightened and glimpses “the bitterness of hell.” But by calling on God he receives strength and commands Satan to leave. Fear is real, but prayer brings power.

f.w: calling upon God, he received strength

n: Satan trembles, the earth shakes, and Moses commands him to depart in the name of the Only Begotten—Christ’s name has power over evil.

f.w: In the name of the Only Begotten, depart hence, Satan

n: Satan leaves weeping, wailing, and gnashing his teeth, and Moses no longer sees him.

f.g: Grinding teeth in rage or anguish.

n: Moses recorded this, but because of wickedness it was lost from the Bible—restored now through Joseph Smith.

f.w: it is not had among the children of men

n: Free of Satan, Moses looks to heaven, filled with the Holy Ghost, who testifies of the Father and the Son.

f.w: the Holy Ghost, which beareth record of the Father and the Son

n: God’s glory returns. God promises Moses will be stronger than many waters, which will obey his command as if he were God—foreshadowing the parting of the Red Sea.
God promises to be with Moses always, for he will deliver Israel from bondage.
Moses sees the entire earth—every particle—discerning it by the Spirit of God.

f.w: discerning it by the Spirit of God

n: He also sees every person on the earth, numberless as sand on the seashore.

f.w: numberless as the sand upon the sea shore

n: He sees many lands, each called earth, with inhabitants—the text may refer to regions of this earth or to other worlds.

f.g: Interpretations vary: lands of this earth or other earths (compare verse 33).

n: Moses asks two great questions: why are these things so, and by what did you make them?

f.g: Moses asks both purpose (why) and means (how).

n: Standing in God’s presence, Moses hears that God made all things for his own purpose—and that wisdom remains with God for now.

f.w: For mine own purpose have I made these things

n: The answer to “by what”: by his word—the Only Begotten Son, full of grace and truth.

f.w: by the word of my power

n: God has created worlds without number, all through his Son.
The first man is called Adam, which means “many”—he is the father of the human family.

f.g: Hebrew ’adam means “man” or “mankind”; here it signifies all humanity.

n: God gives an account only of this earth. Many worlds have passed away, many still exist—countless to us, but each known to God.

f.w: all things are numbered unto me

n: Moses humbly asks to learn about this earth, its people, and the heavens; then he will be content.

f.g: A humble request; Moses accepts God’s limits.

n: The heavens are many and countless to man, but God numbers them all as his own.
As one earth passes away, another comes; God’s works and words are endless.

f.w: there is no end to my works

n: Perhaps the best-known verse in the Pearl of Great Price: God’s work and glory is to bring about the immortality and eternal life of his children. Immortality comes to all through Christ’s resurrection; eternal life is living as God lives.

f.g: Living forever with a resurrected body—given to all through Christ.
Life with God and like God—exaltation.

n: God will now tell Moses about this earth, and Moses must write it down. This introduces the creation account that follows.
People will one day disregard God’s words and remove many from Moses’ book, but God will raise up “another like unto thee” to restore them—understood as Joseph Smith.

f.w: take many of them from the book
I will raise up another like unto thee

n: A note: the mountain’s name will not be known. These words are now given to Joseph Smith and should be shared only with believers—an instruction for that early time.

f.w: Show them not unto any except them that believe
f.g: An early caution; the Book of Moses was later published in full and canonized in 1880.
